title: Birbal and the Goldsmith
summary: A dishonest goldsmith replaces pure gold with brass while making an idol. Birbal uses acid and fire to expose the alloy.
full_text:
An elderly, devout widow named Yashoda saved all her life savings to commission a pure gold statue of a guardian angel to donate to the city temple. She handed thirty tolas of pure, 24-karat gold coins to the chief goldsmith of the bazaar, Seth Hariram, who promised to craft an exquisite idol for twenty silver rupees in labor.

Two months later, the goldsmith delivered the polished statue. It shone with a bright golden gleam.

However, an experienced jeweler who examined the statue whispered to the widow that the idol felt unusually light and had a reddish tint. Suspecting fraud, the widow confronted Hariram, who screamed with rage: 'How dare an illiterate widow insult my sacred craft! I swear on my ancestors that this statue is pure, unadulterated gold!'

The widow wept at Emperor Akbar's feet. Akbar handed the case to Birbal.

Hariram arrived in court, presenting three certificates signed by corrupt bazaar appraisers swearing the gold was pure.

Birbal examined the idol, stroked his chin, and said: 'Hariram, if this statue is indeed thirty tolas of pure gold, you have nothing to fear. We shall verify its purity using the ancient test of the royal mint.'

Birbal ordered a crucible, a charcoal furnace, and bellows brought into the Diwan-i-Khas.

Birbal turned to the widow: 'Mother, if the statue is melted to test its gold, do you consent?'

'Yes, my lord!' the widow replied. 'Better that it be melted into truth than stand in the temple as a monument of deceit!'

The statue was placed into the clay crucible and heated until it melted into glowing liquid. Birbal dropped a lump of pure nitre and borax into the crucible, blowing the flames to white heat.

Dense, foul-smelling black fumes rose from the pot, and thick green slag floated to the surface—the unmistakable sign of cheap copper and brass!

When the impurities burned away and the remaining metal cooled, Birbal weighed the pure gold button on the precision mint scale.

It weighed only twelve tolas! Eighteen tolas of pure gold had been stolen by the goldsmith and replaced with copper alloy!

Hariram fell upon his face, begging for mercy.

Birbal announced the verdict: 'Hariram shall return the thirty tolas of pure gold to the widow, pay an additional thirty tolas as a penalty for defrauding a temple offering, and spend one year in prison!'

Akbar praised Birbal for letting the incorruptible fire speak when human words lied.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Birbal and the Goldsmith"?
options: Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
